query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Micro-alloying equiatomic NbMoTaW with 0.5 at.% Y followed by thermo‐mechanical processing to form a fine, uniform dispersion of ∼20–50 nm Y₂O₃ nanoparticles will enhance room‐temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance without substantially degrading high‐temperature strength or BCC stability.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, homogenized, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.intervention: Add 0.5 at.% Y during melting; thermomechanically process (hot‐rolling + anneal) to precipitate Y₂O₃ nanoparticles.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing at 25 °C and 1600 °C; helium‐ion irradiation (2 MeV He, 1 dpa) at 400 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed Y₂O₃ nanoparticles in the BCC matrix and along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Y₂O₃ particles act as strong sinks for irradiation defects and He, reducing bubble nucleation and growth; they also pin grain boundaries and inhibit crack propagation, increasing ductility; the small volume fraction (<1 %) minimally perturbs the BCC lattice, preserving high‐temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: 1) Room‐temperature tensile elongation increases from ∼5 % to ≥12 %; 2) Yield strength at 1600 °C changes by ≤10 % relative to untreated NbMoTaW; 3) Volumetric void swelling under 1 dpa He irradiation at 400 °C is reduced by ≥50 %.
generation.baseline: Untreated NbMoTaW: RT elongation ∼5 %, yield strength at 1600 °C ∼600 MPa, swelling ∼2 % vol.
generation.boundary: Effective for He implantation energies 0.5–2 MeV, doses up to 1 dpa, temperatures 25–800 °C for irradiation; strength retention evaluated at 1600 °C.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of ductility gain and swelling reduction is estimated from analogous ODS‐W systems; exact values in NbMoTaW–Y₂O₃ are untested.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloys: (A) equiatomic NbMoTaW, (B) NbMoTaW + 0.5 at.% Y; apply identical hot‐rolling and annealing to both. Characterize nanoparticle size and distribution by TEM. Perform tensile tests at 25 °C and 1600 °C. Irradiate both to 1 dpa with 2 MeV He at 400 °C, then measure void swelling by TEM and image analysis.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if Y‐doped alloy shows: (a) RT elongation <10 %, (b) >10 % drop in 1600 °C yield strength relative to base, or (c) <30 % reduction in void swelling compared to untreated NbMoTaW.
